case.dispatchHook: Jacksonville riverfront. Power going places it should not.
briefing: Agent, gadgets along the Jacksonville riverfront started buzzing, glowing, and warming up all at once!
The repair crew needs our help figuring out which energy change each device makes.
Match each device to its energy change, then track down the clues in the field evidence.
Power is on the move across the riverfront, so let's get every circuit humming safely!

lab.intro: Every device transforms energy from one form to another. Match each gadget to the main energy change it makes.

left.name: Desk lamp
left.card: Plugged in, glows bright and feels warm up close

left.name: Speaker
left.card: Plugged in, its cone shakes back and forth

left.name: Electric kettle
left.card: Plugged in, the water inside gets hot

left.name: Solar panel
left.card: Sits in sunlight, a wire runs from it to a light

pairs.why: Spot on! A lamp changes electrical energy into bright light and warmth.
You got it! The fan uses electrical energy to spin its blades into motion.
Spot on! The speaker turns electrical energy into quick vibrations that make sound.
You got it! The electric kettle turns electrical energy into heat to warm the water.
Spot on! The solar panel takes light from the Sun and changes it into electrical energy.

case.debriefClosed: Awesome job, Agent! The riverfront circuits are running smoothly and powered safely again.
case.debriefOpen: This case stays open for now, Agent. Grab your test leads and come back soon to track down that last loose wire!

items.stem: Agent Leo examines six objects that use, store, or give off energy. Which object stores chemical energy?
options: the lamp
the speaker
the battery
the rolling ball
why: A lamp gives off light and heat while glowing. It does not store chemical energy.
A speaker gives off sound energy when it vibrates. It does not store chemical energy.
Spot on! A battery stores chemical energy that can change into electrical energy.
A rolling ball has mechanical energy, which is the energy of motion.
items.alt: Six small pictures: a lamp, a flame, a speaker, a plug, a battery and a rolling ball.
items.tisCheck: Basic forms of energy limited to light, heat, sound, electrical, chemical and mechanical.
items.misconceptions: Batteries thought to hold electricity itself; anything that glows or makes noise seen as storing energy.

items.stem: Agent Maya shines a flashlight at a mirror, and the beam bounces off. Part of the light then goes into a glass of water and bends. Which words name what happens to the light at the mirror and at the water?
options: mirror: reflected; water: refracted
mirror: refracted; water: reflected
mirror: absorbed; water: reflected
mirror: reflected; water: absorbed
why: Spot on! Light that bounces off a mirror is reflected. Light that bends in water is refracted.
Check the terms again! Bouncing off a surface is reflection. Bending as light enters water is refraction.
The mirror bounced the light instead of soaking it up. At the water, the beam bent instead of bouncing.
The mirror reflects the beam, but light that bends in water is refracted rather than absorbed.
keyWords: at the mirror and at the water
items.alt: A flashlight beam hits a mirror and bounces off, and part of the light goes into a glass of water and bends.
items.tisCheck: Light travels in a straight line until it is reflected, refracted or absorbed (SC.3.P.10.3, SC.3.P.10.4).
items.misconceptions: Reflection and refraction swapped; any change in light called absorption.

items.stem: Agent Sam taps four metal bars on a xylophone with the same force. The table shows each bar's length, how fast it vibrates and the pitch of its sound. Which statement is supported by the data?
options: Longer bars vibrate faster and make a higher pitch.
Shorter bars vibrate faster and make a higher pitch.
Hitting a bar harder makes a higher pitch.
All four bars make the same pitch, because they are all metal.
why: Check the table again! The longest bar vibrated slowest and made the lowest pitch.
Spot on! Shorter bars vibrate faster. Faster vibrations produce a higher pitch.
Sam tapped every bar with the same force. Hitting a bar harder changes loudness, not pitch.
Look at the pitch column! The bars make four different pitches from lowest to highest.
items.alt: A table of four xylophone bars: the 20 cm bar vibrates slowest with the lowest pitch, and each shorter bar vibrates faster with a higher pitch, up to the 8 cm bar.
items.tisCheck: Vibrating objects make sound, and pitch depends on how fast they vibrate (SC.4.P.10.3); comparing rows, no computation, no wave terms.
items.misconceptions: Pitch confused with loudness; bigger objects thought to make higher sounds.

items.stem: Agent Leo and Agent Maya checked three things that give off light. They held a hand near each one without touching it. Which statement is supported by what they found?
options: Things that give off light never give off heat.
Only the Sun can give off light and heat at the same time.
Light and heat are the same form of energy.
Things that give off light often give off heat too.
why: Look at the table! All three objects felt warm, so they gave off heat too.
None of these three objects is the Sun, yet every one gave off light and heat.
Light and heat are two different forms of energy, even when an object makes both.
Spot on! The campfire, candle flame, and toaster wires gave off light and felt warm.
items.alt: A table showing that a campfire, a candle flame and glowing toaster wires each give off light and each feel warm nearby.
items.tisCheck: Things that give off light often also give off heat (SC.3.P.11.1); observation without touching.
items.misconceptions: Light and heat seen as one thing; only the Sun thought to give off both.

items.stem: On a 12°C (54°F) morning at the bus stop, Agent Rosa rubs her hands together quickly. After 20 seconds, her hands feel warmer. What made the heat?
options: the sound her hands make
cold air trapped between her hands
her hands rubbing against each other
electrical energy stored in her hands
why: Rubbing hands makes a soft sound, but sound energy does not create warmth.
Cold air cools things down rather than making hands feel warmer.
Spot on! Rubbing two surfaces together creates friction, which makes heat.
Hands do not store electrical energy for heating. The friction from rubbing made the heat.
items.alt: A table showing the agent's hands feel cool before rubbing and warm after 20 seconds of rubbing.
items.tisCheck: Heat produced by rubbing (SC.3.P.11.2); no computation.
items.misconceptions: Warmth credited to sound or to stored energy instead of rubbing.

items.stem: Agent Kai and Agent Sam lay a white shirt and a black shirt in the same sunny spot. The shirts are the same size and fabric. After 30 minutes, the black shirt is much warmer. Why is the black shirt warmer?
options: It reflects more of the light that hits it.
It makes its own heat.
It bends the light, the way water does.
It absorbs more of the light that hits it.
why: Light colors reflect more light away. That is why the white shirt stayed cooler.
Shirts cannot make heat by themselves. The warming energy came from sunlight.
Bending light is refraction. Light does not pass through a shirt like it does through water.
Spot on! Dark colors absorb more light energy, and that absorbed light warms the shirt.
items.alt: A table showing the white shirt at 30°C (86°F) and the black shirt at 38°C (100°F) after 30 minutes in the sun.
items.tisCheck: Light can be absorbed and reflected (SC.3.P.10.4); sunlight is called light only.
items.misconceptions: Dark colors thought to make their own heat; absorbing and reflecting swapped.

items.stem: Agent Maya puts a stick of butter in a pan on a hot stove. In a few minutes, the solid butter turns into a liquid. What caused this change?
options: heat energy from the stove
sound energy from the kitchen
cold air in the room
the shape of the pan
why: Spot on! Heat energy from the stove caused the change, melting solid butter into liquid.
Kitchen sounds do not provide the heat needed to melt butter.
Cold air keeps butter solid. It takes heat energy to melt it.
The pan holds the butter, but heat energy makes it change form.
keyWords: solid butter turns into a liquid
items.alt: A table showing the butter as a solid stick at 0 minutes, soft with melting edges at 2 minutes and liquid at 4 minutes.
items.tisCheck: Energy has the ability to create change (SC.3.P.10.2), with heat as the form; no particle models.
items.misconceptions: Changes seen as happening on their own, without energy.

items.stem: Agent Leo and Agent Rosa watched a sailboat with no motor on the St. Johns River. They wrote down the wind and what the boat did. What does their log show about moving air?
options: The boat moves fastest when the air is calm.
The boat makes the wind when it moves.
Moving air has no effect on the boat.
Moving air has energy that can move the boat.
why: Check the log! The sailboat sat completely still when the air was calm.
The boat has no motor and stayed still until the wind blew. Wind moved the boat.
The boat moved faster as the wind picked up, so moving air definitely had an effect.
Spot on! Stronger wind moved the boat faster, showing moving air has energy to move objects.
items.alt: A table showing the sailboat sat still in calm air, moved slowly in a light breeze and moved fast in a strong wind.
items.tisCheck: Moving air as a source of energy that can move things (SC.4.P.10.4); no computation.
items.misconceptions: Motion thought to cause the wind; moving air not seen as having energy.

items.stem: Agent Sam rolls the same marble down a ramp into an empty paper cup. A marble let go higher on the ramp is moving faster at the bottom. She measures how far the cup slides each time. Which statement explains her results?
options: The cup moves farther when the marble has less energy of motion.
A marble with more energy of motion moves the cup farther.
The height of the ramp has no effect on the cup.
The cup moves because it makes its own energy.
why: Take another look at the table! The slowest marble slid the cup only 5 centimeters.
Spot on! The faster marble had more energy of motion, pushing the cup much farther.
Starting height made a big difference. Higher starting points caused the cup to slide farther.
The cup sat still until the rolling marble hit it and transferred its energy.
items.alt: A table showing the cup slid 5 cm when the marble started low on the ramp, 12 cm from the middle and 20 cm from the top.
items.tisCheck: Energy causes motion (SC.5.P.10.2); mechanical energy described as energy of motion; comparing values only.
items.misconceptions: Objects thought to move on their own energy; speed not linked to energy.

items.stem: Agent Maya and Agent Kai listed four events. In three of them, energy makes something move. Which event shows energy causing a change in a material instead?
options: Wind spins a pinwheel.
A wave lifts a surfboard.
Heat from the Sun dries a wet towel.
A kick sends a ball across the field.
why: Wind makes the pinwheel turn, but the pinwheel itself stays the same material.
The ocean wave moves the surfboard up and down without changing what it is made of.
Spot on! Heat from the Sun evaporates water into vapor, changing the liquid into a gas.
A kick moves the soccer ball across the grass without changing the ball itself.

visual.title: Event Log
rows: a kick sends it across the field

items.alt: A table of four events: wind spins a pinwheel, a wave lifts a surfboard, sunlight dries a wet towel and a kick sends a ball across the field.
items.tisCheck: Energy can cause motion or create change (SC.5.P.10.2); the change shown is water drying, a change of state.
items.misconceptions: Only motion counted as an effect of energy; drying not seen as a change caused by energy.

items.stem: An old mill at a Florida spring has a wooden water wheel. Ranger Diaz and Agent Leo recorded how fast the water flowed and how the wheel moved. Which statement is supported by the log?
options: Moving water has energy that can turn the wheel.
The wheel turns fastest when the water stops.
The wheel makes the water flow.
The wheel would turn the same with no water.
why: Spot on! Faster flowing water spun the wheel faster, proving moving water has energy.
Look at the log! When the water stopped flowing, the wheel stopped turning completely.
Moving water pushes the wheel blades. The wheel does not create the flowing water.
The wheel stayed still when no water flowed. It needs moving water to turn.
items.alt: A table showing the wheel turns fast when the water flows fast, turns slowly when the water flows slowly and does not turn when the water stops.
items.tisCheck: Moving water as a source of energy that can move things (SC.4.P.10.4).
items.misconceptions: The machine thought to move the water; the energy of moving water not recognized.

items.stem: Agent Sam and Agent Maya fly a kite at Jacksonville Beach. When the wind stops, the kite falls. When the wind blows again, the kite rises. What does this show?
options: The kite makes its own energy.
The kite moves the air.
Moving air has energy that can move the kite.
Only moving water has energy.
why: The kite dropped as soon as the wind stopped, so it cannot make its own energy.
The wind pushed the kite up into the sky. The kite does not create the moving air.
Spot on! The kite rises only when the wind blows, showing moving air has energy.
Moving water carries energy, but moving air carries energy too.
items.alt: A table showing the kite rises when the wind blows, falls when the wind stops and rises again when the wind blows again.
items.tisCheck: Moving air as a source of energy that can move things (SC.4.P.10.4).
items.misconceptions: Objects thought to move by their own energy; only water seen as an energy source.

items.stem: Agent Leo tests two circuits with the same battery, wires and bulb. The bulb in Circuit 1 is dark. The bulb in Circuit 2 is lit. Why is only the bulb in Circuit 2 lit?
options: Circuit 2 has a bigger battery.
Circuit 2 is a closed loop, so electricity can flow all the way around.
The open switch in Circuit 1 lets more electricity reach its bulb.
The bulb in Circuit 2 is closer to the battery.
why: Both test circuits use the exact same size battery.
Spot on! A closed switch creates a complete loop, letting electricity flow all the way around.
An open switch creates a break in the circuit, stopping electrical current from reaching the bulb.
Distance along the wire does not matter. The bulb lights only when the circuit is closed.
keyWords: only the bulb in Circuit 2 lit
items.alt: Two circuits with a battery, wires and a bulb: in Circuit 1 the switch is open and the bulb is dark, and in Circuit 2 the switch is closed and the bulb is lit.
items.tisCheck: A closed loop is needed for electricity to flow (SC.5.P.11.1); one simple loop each, no other circuit types, no particle talk.
items.misconceptions: A bigger battery or a shorter distance credited instead of a complete loop; an open switch thought to let more through.

items.stem: Agent Rosa plugs in a blender and presses the button. The blades spin fast. Which energy change does the blender make?
options: motion to electrical
electrical to chemical
sound to electrical
electrical to motion
why: Think about what goes in first! Electrical power enters from the wall, turning into blade motion.
The blender uses electricity to spin its motor. It does not store chemical energy.
The motor makes a buzzing sound, but sound is not the input power driving the blades.
Spot on! The blender takes electrical energy from the wall and transforms it into motion.
items.alt: A table showing nothing moves when the blender is plugged in, and the blades spin fast when the button is pressed.
items.tisCheck: Electrical energy changed into motion, one conversion (SC.5.P.10.4); a non-living system.
items.misconceptions: The direction of the energy change reversed.

items.stem: Agent Maya turns on a flashlight that runs on batteries. The bulb glows. Which list shows the energy changes in order?
options: chemical to electrical to light
light to electrical to chemical
electrical to chemical to sound
mechanical to light to electrical
why: Spot on! Chemical energy in the battery becomes electrical energy, and the bulb produces light.
Check the path of energy! Chemical energy starts in the battery, and light comes out last.
The flashlight makes light rather than sound. Stored chemical energy is the starting point.
There is no mechanical motion starting the flashlight. Chemical energy powers the circuit.

visual.title: Flashlight Parts
rows: carry electricity when the switch is on

items.alt: A table of flashlight parts: the battery stores energy, the wires and switch carry electricity when the switch is on, and the bulb glows.
items.tisCheck: Two energy conversions in one item, the limit (SC.5.P.10.4); a non-living system, no particle talk.
items.misconceptions: The order of the conversions reversed; batteries thought to hold electricity rather than chemical energy.

items.stem: Agent Sam builds a circuit with a gap in it. She bridges the gap with a metal spoon, and the bulb lights. Then she bridges it with a plastic spoon, and the bulb stays dark. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Plastic is a conductor, and metal is an insulator.
Both spoons are conductors, but the plastic spoon is too short.
Metal is a conductor, and plastic is an insulator.
The metal spoon stores electricity for the bulb.
why: Check which spoon worked! Electricity flowed through metal, so metal is the conductor.
Both spoons touched the wires. The bulb stayed dark because plastic blocks electrical flow.
Spot on! Metal conducts electricity to light the bulb, while plastic insulates and blocks current.
The spoon does not store power. It simply allows electricity from the battery to pass through.
items.alt: Two circuits with a gap: a metal spoon bridges one gap and its bulb is lit, and a plastic spoon bridges the other and its bulb is dark.
items.tisCheck: Materials that conduct electricity and those that do not (SC.5.P.11.2); a single loop, no particle talk.
items.misconceptions: Conductor and insulator swapped; conductors thought to store electricity.

items.stem: Agent Kai puts a metal spoon in a mug of hot cocoa. She measures the cocoa and the spoon's handle at the start and again after two minutes. Which way did the heat move?
options: from the spoon into the cocoa
from the cool air into the cocoa
nowhere, because the spoon made its own heat
from the cocoa into the spoon
why: Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things. The spoon started out cooler than the cocoa.
Heat moves outward from hot cocoa into the cooler room air, not the other way around.
The spoon warmed up only because it sat in hot liquid. Spoons cannot create heat.
Spot on! Heat energy travels from the warmer cocoa into the cooler metal spoon.
keyWords: Which way did the heat move
items.alt: A table showing the cocoa at 70°C (158°F) and the spoon handle at 24°C (75°F) at the start, then the cocoa at 66°C (151°F) and the handle at 40°C (104°F) after 2 minutes.
items.tisCheck: Heat flows from hot to cold (SC.4.P.11.1); temperatures in °C with °F, comparing values only, no computation.
items.misconceptions: Cold thought to flow into warm things; the direction of heat flow reversed; objects thought to make their own heat.

items.stem: Agent Rosa rubs two balloons on her hair and hangs them on strings side by side. The balloons push away from each other without touching. Then she holds one balloon near the wall, and it sticks. What makes the two balloons push apart?
options: Both balloons are magnets, with the same poles facing.
Rubbing gave both balloons the same kind of static electricity, so they repel.
Air from the agent's breath pushes the balloons apart.
Gravity pulls each balloon away from the other.
why: Rubber balloons are not magnetic. Rubbing them on hair built up static charges instead.
Spot on! Objects that share the same kind of static charge repel and push apart.
The balloons hang quietly on strings. Static electricity pushes them apart, not moving breath.
Gravity always pulls downward toward Earth, never sideways between hanging balloons.
keyWords: rubs two balloons on her hair
items.alt: A balloon being rubbed on hair, then the same balloon stuck to a wall, with small plus and minus marks.
items.tisCheck: Static electricity can attract or repel without contact (SC.5.P.10.3); framed as static electricity, no particle talk.
items.misconceptions: Static electricity confused with magnetism; a push at a distance credited to air or gravity.

codex.title: Light and heat
codex.line: Things that give off light, like a lamp or a campfire, usually give off heat too.

codex.title: Sound
codex.line: Sound is made when something vibrates, moving quickly back and forth.

codex.title: Solar panel
codex.line: A solar panel changes light from the Sun into electrical energy.
